raw_response:
I've been working this land for 35 years. I know what my fields need. My two sons help when they're back from town, but most of the work falls on me and my wife. Let me think through each crop.

**Wheat and maize — the backbone.** My wheat-maize rotation runs on about 15 mu. I plant wheat in October after the summer maize is off. I'll use the Jimai improved variety the village has been growing for years — I trust it. I put down base fertilizer before planting, then topdress urea at jointing. I'll irrigate four times: once at sowing to get good germination, once before winter sets in, once at jointing, and once at heading. I spray herbicide in winter and a fungicide-insecticide package in spring when the aphids come. After wheat harvest in June, I go straight into maize — no time to waste. I'll use a hybrid seed from the county seed station. Maize I plough less — just rotary till after wheat stubble. Two or three irrigations if the summer rains are short.

**Cotton.** I've grown cotton my whole life. It takes the most work but pays well. I'll put 8 mu into cotton this year. I'll use improved Bt cotton — it cuts down on bollworm spraying somewhat, but I still need to watch it closely. Cotton needs good potassium, so I put more K down here than on the grains. Six pesticide runs at minimum — aphids in early season, bollworm through summer, spider mites when it gets hot and dry.

**Garlic.** My 7 mu of garlic is a cash crop. I plant in October, harvest in May before the wheat comes off. I keep some of my own seed from last year's best bulbs — traditional variety, the white kind that sells well at the local market. Garlic pulls a lot of nutrients from the soil so I fertilize it heavily, especially phosphorus and potassium. I irrigate through the winter and spring. Three or four pesticide applications for leaf blight and thrips.
